scandals.title: Why is it necessary to learn?
scandals.subtitle: The most popular wallets on the market have caused the loss of millions of dollars in Bitcoin—funds that clients believed were completely safe.

ledger.incident: A phished employee let attackers publish a wallet drainer inside the Ledger Connect Kit SDK — roughly $600,000 swept in hours, plus customer-data breaches in 2020 and 2026.

trezor.incident: A laser fault-injection attack on the secure chip in the Safe 7, followed by partner breaches that exposed hundreds of thousands of customer records.

coldcard.incident: A firmware entropy bug made seed phrases predictable. An estimated $88.6M in bitcoin was swept from affected wallets, and updating the firmware does not repair an existing seed.

tangem.incident: A timed laser pulse defeats the card's password-reset check, letting an attacker set a new password. The flaw cannot be patched.

keepkey.incident: Kraken Security Labs pulled the seed phrase out of the device in about fifteen minutes. No firmware fix exists; it needed a hardware redesign.

bitbox02.incident: A firmware update fixed a bootloader flaw and a memory-corruption bug that let a hostile computer run code on the device.

safepal.incident: An order-tracking flaw exposed the names, addresses and phone numbers of roughly 39,798 customers.

ellipal.incident: Ledger Donjon extracted the seed from the air-gapped wallet, defeating the isolation it is sold on.

learningSection.title: Why these wallets fail, and why they will keep failing?
learningSection.body: Your Bitcoin is safe when you have the right knowledge, not when you buy a device. Bitcoin already has the tools, you just need to learn how to use them.

riskScale.title: The risk scale of wallet types
riskScale.subtitle: Highest risk to lowest: from trusting others to verifying your own setup.

custodial.label: Critical
custodial.title: Custodial wallets and exchanges
custodial.body: Your keys live on a server you do not control. The platform can freeze, lose, or leak your funds — and if it fails, you are a creditor, not an owner.

hot.label: High
hot.title: Hot software wallets
hot.body: The keys sit on an online device, next to the apps you install and the links you open. Malware or a convincing page can read them before you notice.

commercial-cold.label: Caution
commercial-cold.title: Commercial cold wallets
commercial-cold.body: The keys stay offline, but the wallet runs firmware you cannot inspect, on hardware heavily exposed to supply chain risks.
commercial-cold.examples: Ledger, Trezor, Tangem, COLDCARD, and similar hardware wallets.

opensource-verifiable.label: Safe
opensource-verifiable.title: Verifiable open-source self-custody
opensource-verifiable.body: You generate and hold your own keys with code you can read and verify, on hardware you control — nothing between you and your coins but your own audit.
